description:
Regenerating a generated artifact that lives in the checkout is invoked the same way for every such artifact, so the repository carries one form of this operation rather than two.

## Background

Several files in this repository are generated into the working tree and committed: reference documents rendered from engine declarations, and marked regions rendered from a packaged authority. Each has an assertion that fails when the committed bytes drift from what its source now renders, and each needs a way for a contributor to bring the committed bytes back into agreement.

Two shapes of that second half now exist. Six generators are `#[ignore]`d tests beside their asserting sibling, regenerated by naming the ignored test on a cargo command line, or in one case by setting an environment variable while running the assertion itself: `crates/jit/src/gate_presets/reference.rs`, `crates/jit/src/runtime_defaults.rs`, `crates/jit/src/domain/event_catalog.rs`, `crates/jit/src/output.rs`, `crates/jit/src/storage/reference.rs`, and `crates/jit/src/schema.rs`. Two generators added by this container are shell entry points under the script directory, each taking no arguments, printing what it did, and distinguishing "already current" from "refused or could not run" by exit status.

Both shapes satisfy the property that matters most — neither writes during a default test run — so this is not a correctness gap. It is a single operation with two interfaces, which `@/invariant/convention-convergence` names as a defect rather than a matter of taste: a contributor who learns one shape does not thereby know how to regenerate anything using the other, and a reviewer cannot tell from a call site which applies.

The shell entry point is the form to converge on, and the reason is reach rather than preference. It is the only shape available to a generator whose values come from running a built binary rather than from calling library code, which is why this container's documentation-region generator has it; a generator expressed only as an ignored test could not be written that way at all. It also names itself: a directory listing of the script directory enumerates what can be regenerated, where the ignored tests are discoverable only by knowing they exist.

What sits behind the entry point stays free. One generator runs an installed binary against a throwaway directory; another compiles the crate and runs a program that calls the render directly. That difference follows from where each artifact's authority lives and is not part of the convention.

Two constraints bound how this is done. The build-footprint budget counts integration-test targets against a ceiling with one slot free, and sums the bytes of executables built with the test profile; a migration that adds one compiled target per generator spends footprint for no gain, so the target count this adds is a design decision to make deliberately rather than a consequence to discover. And every asserting sibling must survive the migration unweakened — the assertion is what makes drift visible, and the entry point only repairs it.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Every generated artifact that is written into the checkout and committed is regenerated through the same kind of entry point, invoked the same way, with the same convention for reporting that it changed nothing, changed something, or could not run.
- [hard] REQ-02: The six generators presently expressed as ignored tests or as an environment-gated branch of an assertion are reachable through that entry point.
- [hard] REQ-03: No generator writes into the checkout during a default test run, and a full default test run leaves the working tree clean.
- [hard] REQ-04: Every generated artifact retains an assertion that fails when the committed bytes differ from what its source renders, and the failure names the command that regenerates it.
- [hard] REQ-05: The regeneration path and the assertion for a given artifact read one implementation of its render, so the two cannot disagree.
- [hard] REQ-06: The build-footprint budget's integration-target and executable-byte assertions hold, and the number of compiled targets the migration adds is stated with its reasoning rather than left implicit.
- [hard] REQ-07: A contributor can enumerate what this repository can regenerate, and how, from one place.
- [hard] REQ-08: A regeneration run immediately following a first one reports that it changed nothing, for every artifact.

## Notes

Preserving each generated artifact's byte content is the measure of a correct migration: this changes how regeneration is invoked, not what any generator produces. A migrated generator that alters its output has a defect, whichever side is wrong.

Publication that stages a file and renames it must carry the destination's existing permissions onto the staged file. A temporary file is created owner-only, and git does not track that bit, so a generator that skips this leaves a mode change no diff reveals.

Owner-directed addition (2026-07-31, execution-lead escalation): the container's own work introduced the second shape, and the owner ruled that convergence is mandatory inside this container rather than deferred to a tracked follow-up, so `@/invariant/convention-convergence` holds without an exception.
title: Regenerating a checked-in generated artifact has one invocation form
